## Proof

We wish to determine whether there exist an **irrational** number $\alpha$ and a **rational** number $r\neq 0$ such that
$$\alpha^{r}=2^{e}.$$

Equivalently (taking the unique positive real $r$-th root), we need
$$\alpha = 2^{\,e/r}\notin\mathbb{Q}.$$

---

### A useful subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$

Let
$$G:=\log_{2}\!\bigl(\mathbb{Q}^{>0}\bigr)=\{\log_{2}q:q\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}\}.$$
By unique factorization, every positive rational $q$ is uniquely $\prod p^{n_p}$ ($n_p\in\mathbb{Z}$, finitely many nonzero), so
$$G=\bigoplus_{p\ \text{prime}}\mathbb{Z}\,\log_{2}p.$$
The generators $\{\log_{2}p\}$ are **$\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent**: if $\sum q_{p}\log_{2}p=0$ with $q_{p}\in\mathbb{Q}$, clearing denominators gives $\sum a_{p}\log_{2}p=0$ ($a_{p}\in\mathbb{Z}$), i.e. $\prod p^{a_{p}}=1$, forcing every $a_{p}=0$. Hence every element of $G$ has a **unique** representation $\sum n_{p}\log_{2}p$ with $n_{p}\in\mathbb{Z}$.

The key equivalence is:
$$2^{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}\iff x\in G.$$
(If $x\in G$, then $x=\log_{2}q$ and $2^{x}=q\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}$; conversely if $2^{x}=q\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}$, then $x=\log_{2}q\in G$.)

So $\alpha=2^{e/r}$ is irrational **iff** $e/r\notin G$.

---

### Two cases

**Case 1: $e\notin G$.**  
Then $e/2\notin G$ either, since $G$ is closed under multiplication by $2$ (if $e/2\in G$, then $e=2\cdot(e/2)\in G$, contradiction). Set $r=2$ and $\alpha=2^{e/2}$. Then $\alpha\notin\mathbb{Q}$ and
$$\alpha^{2}=\bigl(2^{e/2}\bigr)^{2}=2^{e}.$$

**Case 2: $e\in G$.**  
Write the unique representation
$$e=\sum_{i=1}^{m}n_{i}\log_{2}p_{i},\qquad n_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\},$$
with distinct primes $p_{i}$. (Not all $n_{i}$ are zero because $e\neq 0$.) Choose an integer $k\ge 2$ such that $k\nmid n_{j}$ for some index $j$ — for instance $k=2$ if some $n_{i}$ is odd, otherwise take any $k>\max_{i}|n_{i}|$. Set $r=k$ and $\alpha=2^{e/k}$. Then
$$\frac{e}{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{n_{i}}{k}\log_{2}p_{i}.$$
If $e/k\in G$, uniqueness of the representation in $G$ would force every $n_{i}/k\in\mathbb{Z}$, i.e. $k\mid n_{i}$ for all $i$ — contradicting the choice of $k$. Hence $e/k\notin G$, so $\alpha=2^{e/k}\notin\mathbb{Q}$, and
$$\alpha^{k}=\bigl(2^{e/k}\bigr)^{k}=2^{e}.$$

---

### Conclusion

In **every** case we have produced an irrational $\alpha$ and a nonzero rational $r$ (in fact $r\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}$, so the power is nontrivial) with $\alpha^{r}=2^{e}$. The argument is unconditional — it does not require knowing whether $2^{e}$ itself is rational, algebraic, or transcendental (which is in fact an open problem, since Gelfond–Schneider does not apply to the transcendental exponent $e$).

Therefore **yes**, $2^{e}$ can be expressed as an irrational number raised to a rational power. $\blacksquare$

## Proof

We wish to determine whether there exist an **irrational** number $\alpha$ and a **rational** number $r\neq 0$ such that
$$\alpha^{r}=2^{e}.$$

Equivalently (taking the unique positive real $r$-th root), we need
$$\alpha = 2^{\,e/r}\notin\mathbb{Q}.$$

---

### A useful subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$

Let
$$G:=\log_{2}\!\bigl(\mathbb{Q}^{>0}\bigr)=\{\log_{2}q:q\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}\}.$$
By unique factorization, every positive rational $q$ is uniquely $\prod p^{n_p}$ ($n_p\in\mathbb{Z}$, finitely many nonzero), so
$$G=\bigoplus_{p\ \text{prime}}\mathbb{Z}\,\log_{2}p.$$
The generators $\{\log_{2}p\}$ are **$\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent**: if $\sum q_{p}\log_{2}p=0$ with $q_{p}\in\mathbb{Q}$, clearing denominators gives $\sum a_{p}\log_{2}p=0$ ($a_{p}\in\mathbb{Z}$), i.e. $\prod p^{a_{p}}=1$, forcing every $a_{p}=0$. Hence every element of $G$ has a **unique** representation $\sum n_{p}\log_{2}p$ with $n_{p}\in\mathbb{Z}$.

The key equivalence is:
$$2^{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}\iff x\in G.$$
(If $x\in G$, then $x=\log_{2}q$ and $2^{x}=q\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}$; conversely if $2^{x}=q\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}$, then $x=\log_{2}q\in G$.)

So $\alpha=2^{e/r}$ is irrational **iff** $e/r\notin G$.

---

### Two cases

**Case 1: $e\notin G$.**  
Then $e/2\notin G$ either, since $G$ is closed under multiplication by $2$ (if $e/2\in G$, then $e=2\cdot(e/2)\in G$, contradiction). Set $r=2$ and $\alpha=2^{e/2}$. Then $\alpha\notin\mathbb{Q}$ and
$$\alpha^{2}=\bigl(2^{e/2}\bigr)^{2}=2^{e}.$$

**Case 2: $e\in G$.**  
Write the unique representation
$$e=\sum_{i=1}^{m}n_{i}\log_{2}p_{i},\qquad n_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\},$$
with distinct primes $p_{i}$. (Not all $n_{i}$ are zero because $e\neq 0$.) Choose an integer $k\ge 2$ such that $k\nmid n_{j}$ for some index $j$ — for instance $k=2$ if some $n_{i}$ is odd, otherwise take any $k>\max_{i}|n_{i}|$. Set $r=k$ and $\alpha=2^{e/k}$. Then
$$\frac{e}{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{n_{i}}{k}\log_{2}p_{i}.$$
If $e/k\in G$, uniqueness of the representation in $G$ would force every $n_{i}/k\in\mathbb{Z}$, i.e. $k\mid n_{i}$ for all $i$ — contradicting the choice of $k$. Hence $e/k\notin G$, so $\alpha=2^{e/k}\notin\mathbb{Q}$, and
$$\alpha^{k}=\bigl(2^{e/k}\bigr)^{k}=2^{e}.$$

---

### Conclusion

In **every** case we have produced an irrational $\alpha$ and a nonzero rational $r$ (in fact $r\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}$, so the power is nontrivial) with $\alpha^{r}=2^{e}$. The argument is unconditional — it does not require knowing whether $2^{e}$ itself is rational, algebraic, or transcendental (which is in fact an open problem, since Gelfond–Schneider does not apply to the transcendental exponent $e$).

Therefore **yes**, $2^{e}$ can be expressed as an irrational number raised to a rational power. $\blacksquare$
